- # Why the eyes drift during fixation {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} + # Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in Chapters 1 and 2 stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation] - ## Why a small correlation implies shared variation {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} + ## The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain. It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are $N_m$ independent single neuron predictors $X_i$. Standardize each to variance one and also standardize $Y$. Independence makes the $X_i$ uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. $$ Consequently $\sum_iR_i^2\le1$, and an average neuron explains at most $1/N_m$. This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.[^p2-independent-bound] The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, $$ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. $$ Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%; for several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source. Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.[^p2-independent-bound] This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.[^p2-independence] - ## The fraction driven by the common command {#sec:EYE-CHI} + ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the fact that the inverse filter has a calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The assumptions are that the common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale, and that $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows exactly what those assumptions buy: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there. **Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise. The constructed variance example above gives a small correlation even though the common command supplies most of the movement variance.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
Private prediction noise enlarges the denominator of R without changing the covariance. The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. The reported result was $0.82\pm0.07$, a weighted mean and weighted error for horizontal displacement over 350 ms. It is neither a fraction of distance traveled nor the fraction that one neuron's spikes accurately predict.[^p2-chi-error] - ## Separating measurement noise from movement in the MSD {#sec:EYE-MEASUREMENT-NOISE} + ## Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD {#sec:EYE-MEASUREMENT-NOISE} The common variance calculation uses one interval length. To learn what kind of process drives motion, the authors next compare displacements at many time separations. As in Chapter 1, $$ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} $$ is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag $\ell$. The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.[^p2-msd] At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil's measurement error. Suppose its reading is $E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)$, where the measurement error has zero mean, variance $\sigma_m^2$, is independent of true movement, and is uncorrelated between distinct sampled times. For a positive lag, $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta\nu)^2]\\ &=M(\ell)+\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)^2]+\mathbb E[\nu(t)^2] -2\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)\nu(t)]\\ &=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, $2\sigma_m^2$, rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.[^p2-msd-noise] The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order $10^{-3}$ deg$^2$, checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial's unknown noise. Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty $10^{-4}$ deg$^2$, a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.[^p2-noise-limit] For instance, a constructed measured MSD of $0.0014$ deg$^2$ with an estimated noise contribution $0.0010$ deg$^2$ leaves $0.0004$ deg$^2$. A $0.0001$ deg$^2$ uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be $2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]$, where $C_\nu$ is their covariance at lag $\ell$; a constant subtraction would then need revision. For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
{{block:fig:EYE-MSD-MEASUREMENT-OFFSET}}
The offset comes from two independent position errors, one at each endpoint. Its removal changes the average MSD; it does not recover each trajectory’s unknown error. The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). - ## Filtering white noise and filtering Brownian motion differ {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} + ## The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. $$ Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags; it does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.[^p2-msd-result] Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones. [**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time. A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation. Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where $$ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). $$ The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. $$ For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives $$ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. $$ If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). $$ This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result] Now suppose the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. Let $$ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives $$ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. After its velocity transient has decayed, its solution is $$ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u), \qquad C_v(s)=\frac D\tau e^{-|s|/\tau}. $$ The covariance follows by multiplying the two integrals: only their shared increments contribute, with the same exponential overlap as in the white noise calculation. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} $$ At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. $$ The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), $$ which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Its local slope is $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, $$ approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$; at $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit. The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
{{block:fig:EYE-FILTERED-NOISE-MSD}}
The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. A slow correlated peripheral source is a different hypothesis from the temporally uncorrelated noise rejected by this comparison. - ## The proposed circuit from memory to movement {#sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL} + ## A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering {#sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL} The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. There are two populations, with excitation within each and inhibition between them. Their firing increases for opposite directions of gaze. This supplies the recurrent interaction needed to maintain a range of stored positions.[^p2-network] For the right population, the model's rate is $$ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). $$ $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$. Spikes produce synaptic activity according to $$ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. $$ Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially; one spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network] The readout $E_{OI}$ feeds back into the rates, so these equations define a recurrent network. Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set $F=0$ and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value $z$ by $$ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. $$ Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same $\tau_s$ applies to every unit, the readout obeys $$ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. $$ An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require $G(z)=z$ over the represented range. For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives $$ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. $$ Thus $G'(z)=1$ is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum. The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction additionally accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper's equations; Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.[^p2-network] The motor neurons receive this position signal: $$ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. $$ $\lambda_i^M$ is a motor rate in spikes/s, $E_{T_i}$ is that neuron's position threshold in degrees, and $k_i$ is its position sensitivity. $\xi_i^M$ is its generated spike train. The filtered output $s_i^M$ also has units spikes/s, with decay time $\tau_{MN}$. One spike makes a jump of $1/\tau_{MN}$; at constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate. Each motor unit's muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution $E_i$ satisfying $$ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. $$ These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant $E_{OI}$, an active unit has mean $s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})$, giving mean $E_i=E_{OI}$ when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.[^p2-motor] The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between $-45$ and $-5$ degrees, and imposed $m_i {{block:tbl:EYE-FIGURE-GUIDE}} The most useful supplemental comparisons are Extended Data Fig. 1 for individual uncertainty, Fig. 2 for noise subtraction and its simulated control, Fig. 3 for feedback, Fig. 4 for a no-central-drive control, and Fig. 5 for the other monkey's fit. In the no-central-drive control, $\widehat\chi=-0.09\pm0.22$ is compatible with zero; that negative estimate is sampling variation. Figures 6–8 document cell classification, segment sampling, and a rank correlation check. Figure 9 shows the heterogeneous model parameters. Figure 10 separates spiking noise passed directly to the output from spiking noise that drives diffusion inside the integrator: internal stochastic spikes remain in the latter comparison. Its caption reports little direct output-noise effect beyond 50 ms.[^p2-supp-figures] - ## What remains uncertain {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} + ## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} The data and model answer different localization questions. The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions. The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter. The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing. Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. No integrator neurons were recorded in this study. No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift. Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.[^p2-localization] The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. folds.title: Derivation: normalization and higher size moments
folds.text:
Normalization needs no special integral: $\int_0^\infty p_d(s)\,ds=\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,du=1$. The same substitution supplies every positive moment,

$$
\mathbb E[s^k]
=\beta^{-kd/2}\int_0^\infty u^{kd/2}e^{-u}\,du
=\beta^{-kd/2}\Gamma(1+kd/2).
$$

folds.title: Source check: three printed steps in the supplement
folds.text: **Reading the supplement carefully.** The printed supplement appears to contain algebraic errors in this calculation. Its Equation S18 prints multiplication by mean size where the preceding moment formula requires division. Its Equation S23 omits a factor $\sqrt2$ when solving the parabola in S22 for full width. In S25 the finite-height quadratic exponent should be negative. The derivation above retains the main paper's distributional form and obtains the constants from the displayed parabola, the moment integral, and the independent crossing calculation. These corrections concern the printed derivation; they do not establish that the simulation code or empirical fits used the same mistakes.[^p3-corrections]

folds.title: Independent check: recover field width from its boundary slope
folds.text:
There is also an independent check on the high threshold width constant. Starting at an upcrossing with slope $v$, the local excursion is approximately

$$
z(x)-q\simeq vx-\frac{q}{2\sigma^2}x^2.
$$

Its second root is $s=2\sigma^2v/q$. Changing variables in the exact crossing slope law gives $p(s)=2\beta s e^{-\beta s^2}$ with $\beta=q^2/(8\sigma^2)$, the same constant as the peak calculation for $v_1=2$.

folds.title: Derivation: the Gaussian determinant average and its integrals
folds.text:
Here are the Gaussian algebra steps behind the determinant average. Write the conditional Hessian as $H=-b\lambda I+G$, where $G$ has zero mean. Differentiating an isotropic covariance four times gives, for distinct indices $i,k$,

$$
\mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}]=\kappa-\lambda^2,
\qquad
\mathbb E[G_{ik}^2]=\kappa.
$$

The constant $\kappa$ describes a fourth derivative of covariance. Conditioning on height subtracts $\lambda^2$ from the covariance of the two diagonal entries, but not from the off-diagonal variance. Hence each pair contributes

$$
\mathbb E[G_{ii}G_{kk}-G_{ik}^2]=-\lambda^2.
$$

For $j=1$, $\mathbb E[\det(-H)\mid b]=b\lambda$. For $j=2$, expand the two by two determinant to obtain $\lambda^2(b^2-1)$. For $j=3$, the leading term is $b^3\lambda^3$; the three index pairs each contribute $-b\lambda^3$, and all odd centered Gaussian products vanish. The result is $\lambda^3(b^3-3b)$. The unknown fourth derivative $\kappa$ has canceled.

Integrating the three polynomials gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_q^\infty b\phi(b)\,db&=\phi(q),\\
\int_q^\infty(b^2-1)\phi(b)\,db&=q\phi(q),\\
\int_q^\infty(b^3-3b)\phi(b)\,db&=(q^2-1)\phi(q).
\end{aligned}
$$

For example, differentiate $-q\phi(q)$ to get $(q^2-1)\phi(q)$, which verifies the second integral using its vanishing upper endpoint. Combining the determinant, gradient density, and integral gives the signed densities above.

- # Why place fields have different sizes and shapes {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} + # A thresholded Gaussian map predicts field sizes and shapes {#ch:PLACE-FIELDS} A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions? Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak propose that a cell's spatial input is a smooth random function. The cell fires where this function exceeds a threshold. The model predicts distributions of field lengths, areas, and volumes, rather than the location of a particular cell's next field. Its strongest tests ask whether fitting field sizes and counts also explains field shapes and holes.[^p3-question] This chapter develops the calculations behind that claim. Spatial randomness here describes different possible rate maps. Once a map is drawn, it is fixed while the animal moves through it. The spatial coordinate is not time, and the model does not by itself describe memory drift, spike timing, or learning. - ## From a rate map to a random function {#sec:PLACE-GP} + ## Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields {#sec:PLACE-GP} To predict a field's width, we need to relate activity at nearby positions. A histogram of firing rates alone loses that information: rearranging its values could turn one broad field into many tiny fields without changing the histogram. A [**Gaussian process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a probability distribution over functions such that the values at any finite set of positions form a jointly Gaussian random vector. For positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, the vector $(h(x_1),\ldots,h(x_n))$ therefore has a multivariate Gaussian distribution. Its mean vector and covariance matrix are obtained by evaluating two functions, $$ m(x)=\mathbb E[h(x)],\qquad C(x,y)=\mathbb E[(h(x)-m(x))(h(y)-m(y))]. $$ The expectation runs over possible maps, or over cells assumed to share these statistics. Model histogram error bars come from $10^4$ simulations matched to the number of recorded cells; they do not quantify every source of animal-level or measurement uncertainty.[^p3-fit-tests] The processing choices affect the quantities being compared. - # Relating spatial codes, memory, and behavior {#ch:SYNTHESIS} + # Spatial maps and memory dynamics need separate tests {#ch:SYNTHESIS} A model can explain the shape of a neural code without explaining how that code is maintained. It can also explain fluctuations inside a circuit without uniquely locating the source of a measured behavior. The three papers become more useful together when these different claims are kept attached to their actual mathematical and experimental tests. - ## Three questions about one represented quantity {#sec:SYNTHESIS-QUESTIONS} + ## The three papers constrain maps, dynamics, and movement {#sec:SYNTHESIS-QUESTIONS} For a circuit representing position, three questions arise. What activity pattern corresponds to each position? How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The place-field model addresses the first question. The persistent-activity model addresses the second. The eye-drift model combines a candidate answer to the second with a detailed answer to the third.[^s-three] The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, $\theta(t)$ locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, $x$ locates an animal in an environment, and $h_i(x)$ is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered $x$ through time. The [guide map](ch-foundations.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) gives a visual comparison of these three questions.
{{block:tbl:SYNTHESIS-MODELS}}
The 2012 and 2022 connection is direct: neural noise can move a maintained eye-position command, which then drives muscles. The 2022 result provides evidence for a substantial shared source before the final motor neurons and shows that integrator diffusion is sufficient within the constructed model. It does not measure the circuit's Fisher information or test equality in the 2012 bound. The 2025 connection is broader: an internally coherent position estimate can be expressed through spatially irregular tuning curves. ## How a static map can carry a moving estimate {#sec:SYNTHESIS-JOINT-CALCULATION} Suppose a network maintains a one-dimensional estimate $x(t)$ and cell $i$ has a fixed expected-rate function $f_i(x)$. Its time-dependent expected rate is $$ R_i(t)=f_i(x(t)). $$ Here $f_i$ describes spatial tuning and $x(t)$ describes dynamics. A source of time variation has entered even though $f_i$ is fixed. Actual spike counts add another layer of variability around the expected rate. This construction is a guide calculation connecting the papers' objects, not a model tested jointly by the three studies. Consider a short interval of duration $t$ starting at $x_0$. Assume that the estimate's local displacement $\delta x=x(t)-x_0$ has mean zero and variance $2Dt$, and that it is small enough to linearize each rate curve. Taylor expansion gives $$ f_i(x_0+\delta x) =f_i(x_0)+f_i'(x_0)\delta x+O((\delta x)^2). $$ To leading order, the change is $\delta R_i=f_i'(x_0)\delta x$. Multiplying the centered changes for neurons $i$ and $j$ and averaging yields $$ \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_i,\delta R_j) \simeq f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0)\operatorname{Var}(\delta x) =2Dt\,f_i'(x_0)f_j'(x_0). $$ This covariance concerns expected-rate changes caused by the common represented displacement, conditional on the starting position. It is not a formula for every covariance in a spiking recurrent network. It neglects higher-order changes in tuning and additional private or shared fluctuations. Near a threshold or over a large spatial displacement, the linear approximation must be revisited. ### Example: opposite rate changes from the same position error {#sec:SYNTHESIS-COVARIANCE-EXAMPLE} Let the local slopes of two rate curves be $f_1'=2$ Hz/m and $f_2'=-1$ Hz/m. Suppose $D=0.01$ m²/s and the interval is 0.5 s. Then the variance of the common position displacement is $2Dt=0.01$ m². The contributions to rate variance and covariance are $$ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_1)=2^2(0.01)=0.04\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_2)=(-1)^2(0.01)=0.01\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_1,\delta R_2)=(2)(-1)(0.01) =-0.02\ \mathrm{Hz}^2. $$ With only this one source, the two rate changes have correlation $-1$: one rises whenever the other falls. Adding independent private noise lowers the magnitude. The negative covariance here comes from opposite tuning slopes under a common position change. It does not establish an inhibitory connection between the cells. For the same slopes, set both expected rates to 10 Hz at the starting position. The upper plot shows the fixed rate curves; the lower plot shows their changes under a common position displacement.
{{block:fig:SYNTHESIS-SHARED-POSITION}}
Both changes are set by the same position displacement, so they occupy one direction in the two-rate plane. Independent private fluctuations would spread them away from that line. This example explains why irregular or mixed single-cell responses can coexist with a low-dimensional population fluctuation. It also shows the extra evidence required to connect a spatial map to a dynamical mechanism: one must measure how population changes align with the directions implied by those maps, rather than infer dynamics from field shapes alone. - ## What makes an experimental test restrictive {#sec:SYNTHESIS-EVIDENCE} + ## Each model needs a test matched to its claim {#sec:SYNTHESIS-EVIDENCE} A model that matches one distribution may have enough adjustable parameters to do so for several different reasons. The place-field paper gains support by fitting arrangement parameters and then comparing additional features, including slices and shape statistics. The separate firing-rate multiplier used in some comparisons should remain visible when counting how many quantities were predicted without further fitting. A successful high-threshold formula is also a statement about its limiting assumptions; finite-threshold simulations and the original recordings provide different kinds of checks. The eye paper uses a different strategy. It calibrates a movement-to-firing relationship, inverts it, and compares the resulting single-neuron displacement predictions with measured displacement. Shared covariance then carries information that independent private fluctuations cannot supply under the decomposition's assumptions. The additional MSD comparison tests the time structure: increasing stationary motor-noise amplitude cannot by itself reproduce the accumulating upstream signal. Calibration validity, source correlations, two animals, and horizontal movement remain part of the result's scope. The 2012 inequality is a mathematical constraint rather than an experimental fit. Its derivation specifies what noise and dynamics it covers. An experimental comparison would need estimates of diffusion, the relevant time constants, and the appropriate instantaneous information rate, all under compatible conditions. Agreement with $1/N$ scaling alone would not test the entire inequality, since several mechanisms can share that scaling. - ## Related work and what it changes {#sec:SYNTHESIS-RELATED} + ## Related studies change assumptions and leave circuit choices open {#sec:SYNTHESIS-RELATED} The foundational eye-position account is Seung's line-attractor model. Aksay and colleagues then used recordings and perturbations in goldfish to constrain integrator circuitry. These establish the dynamical problem and experimental architecture behind the 2022 model. Neither supplies the macaque displacement-variance estimate. Burak and Fiete's earlier grid-cell study puts a related integrator problem in navigation: recurrent population activity is driven by velocity and accumulates path-integration errors. Its accuracy ranges belong to the simulated networks and parameter choices, rather than all biological grid circuits.[^s-attractors] Noise-driven storage also connects to memory capacity. Koyluoglu and colleagues ask how noise limits recall as the delay and number of stored items increase. Their comparison with human data shows why direct storage of several independent values need not capture observed behavior; transformations before and after storage alter the performance prediction. Seeholzer and colleagues examine how short-term changes in synaptic strength affect diffusion and systematic drift. These papers change the storage assumptions rather than invalidate the 2012 calculation inside its original model.[^s-extensions] For place fields, Eliav and colleagues' long-tunnel recordings and Harland and colleagues' large-arena recordings supply the multiple-field, multiple-scale observations. Yartsev and Ulanovsky supply the three-dimensional bat recordings. The 2025 paper reanalyzes those existing data, so its agreement across dimensions is not three newly collected experiments under one protocol. The later study by Maimon and colleagues directly compares CA3 and CA1 in large tunnels: predominantly single fields in CA3 contrast with multiple fields in CA1, while field sizes are similar. That distinction supports treating the CA1 statistics and the upstream spatial circuit as related but separately constrained parts of the explanation.[^s-place-data] There are also direct reasons to avoid reading Gaussian spatial statistics as a unique wiring diagram. Druckmann and colleagues report structured synaptic connectivity between hippocampal regions. Bittner and colleagues show how electrical events in dendrites, the branching input structures of neurons, can induce changes in synaptic strength and form CA1 place fields. Structure and learning can therefore be present even when a random-function model describes many aggregate field statistics. The model's success leaves open which circuit mechanism produces these maps. Input, connectivity, learning, or perturbation measurements could distinguish the possibilities.[^s-wiring] Finally, the source and use of eye motion are different questions. Nghiem and colleagues combine human eye tracking with a model of how eye movement affects visual signals to explain why an intermediate amount of fixational motion can help fine visual discrimination. A movement that partly originates from internal noise can still have useful sensory consequences, and feedback can regulate its statistics. Benefit for perception does not uniquely identify the neural generator.[^s-acuity] - ## A joint comparison that remains to be done {#sec:SYNTHESIS-NEXT} + ## A joint test would compare tuning maps with population fluctuations {#sec:SYNTHESIS-NEXT} The combined calculation suggests a concrete research direction. For the same population, first estimate the tuning maps with their uncertainty. Then measure fluctuations during periods where external anchoring is weak and test whether their covariance is aligned with changes along those maps. Fit diffusion only over a range where the local approximation and measurement corrections are justified. A downstream behavioral comparison must additionally include the physical or neural filters between representation and measurement. This would ask whether one system satisfies both spatial-statistics and dynamical-stability constraints. A static Gaussian-process fit alone cannot supply the diffusion coefficient. A diffusion fit alone cannot establish the distribution of fields. A joint success would be more restrictive, while a mismatch would point to a particular assumption to change: spatial input statistics, recurrent maintenance, the observation filter, or their coupling.
